results.title: Together AI raises reserved H100 pricing while expanding its model catalog — PricingSaaS Pulse
highlights:
## What changed

Together AI raised reserved-cluster pricing for NVIDIA HGX H100 GPUs across every commitment tier: 31-90 days moved from $3.59 to $3.69/GPU/hr, 91-180 days from $3.29 to $3.45/GPU/hr, and 181+ days from $3.09 to $3.19/GPU/hr. On-demand H100 pricing held flat at $3.99/hr. Separately, Together added two serverless inference models to its catalog: Kimi K3 at $3.00/$15.00 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.30 cached) and Inkling Small at $0.50/$1.20 per 1M tokens ($0.10 cached).

## Why it matters

Reserved-GPU price increases from a major neocloud are a leading indicator for compute costs across the AI stack. Watch whether other GPU cloud providers such as CoreWeave, Lambda, and Crusoe follow with their own reserved-tier increases in the coming weeks, and whether Togethers on-demand rate holds or eventually follows the reserved tiers upward.

## In context

That the increase hits every reserved tier but leaves on-demand pricing untouched suggests reserved capacity, not spot demand, is where H100 supply is actually tight; providers typically raise on-demand rates first when demand is the binding constraint. Layering in two new serverless models the same period is a bundling move to keep customers engaged with the platform even as compute becomes more expensive to reserve.

results.title: Reserve GPU Compute Now: Why Waiting Could Cost You 40% or More in 2026 | Source GPU
highlights:
H100 rental pricing rose almost 40 percent in five months. On-demand capacity is sold out across every major GPU type. If you're still waiting for a better moment to lock in compute, the data says that moment already passed.

...

## 1. The Price Move Already Happened, and It's Still Moving

H100 1-year reserved rental pricing climbed from roughly $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 per GPU-hour by March 2026, an increase of almost 40 percent in five months. That's not a one-time correction. AWS raised H200 capacity-block pricing again in January 2026, this time by roughly 15 percent, with nothing in the underlying hardware or power cost changing at all. The increase was pure scarcity premium, providers charging more simply because demand for the same fixed supply kept climbing.

On-demand GPU rental capacity has been effectively sold out across every major chip type since early 2026. Teams that already hold on-demand instances aren't releasing that capacity back into the market even as prices rise around them, which means the squeeze isn't temporary friction, it's the market finding a new, higher equilibrium with less room in it than before.

...

The gap between reserved and on-demand pricing has widened into one of the clearest cost decisions in enterprise compute today. Long-term reservations commonly run 40 to 70 percent cheaper per hour than on-demand rates for the same hardware. Where on-demand H100 pricing hovers between $2.50 and $5.00 an hour depending on provider, reserved access to that same chip can bring the effective rate down to $1.00 to $2.00 an hour.

That spread exists because the on-demand price is effectively a queue price, what a provider charges when supply is genuinely scarce and demand is immediate. The reserved price is closer to the provider's actual supply forecast, discounted because they're getting certainty in exchange for a lower margin. In a market this tight, on-demand pricing captures the full scarcity premium every single hour. Reserving locks in a rate before the next price move happens, not after.

...

| Factor | On-Demand | Reserved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical H100 rate | $2.50 to $5.00 per GPU-hour | $1.00 to $2.00 per GPU-hour |
| Availability risk | High, most pools are effectively sold out | Lower, capacity is allocated ahead of need |
| Price exposure | Full exposure to future scarcity premiums | Rate locked for the reservation term |
| Best for | Short, unpredictable, or bursty workloads | Sustained or planned workloads of known duration |

results.title: On-Demand vs. Reserved GPU Rental: What Actually Saves Money in 2026's Tight Market | Source GPU
highlights:
Reserved GPU pricing can cut your rate by 40 to 70 percent, but only if your utilization clears a specific threshold. Get that math wrong and reserved capacity becomes the more expensive option, not the cheaper one. Here's the actual decision framework.

...

## 1. The Real Price Gap Right Now

On-demand H100 pricing typically runs $2.50 to $5.00 per GPU-hour, depending on provider, with hyperscaler on-demand rates often landing at the high end of that range or above it. Reserved access to the same chip commonly brings that down to $1.00 to $2.00 per hour, with major cloud providers advertising up to 70 to 72 percent off on-demand rates for longer commitments.

On a modest cluster of 16 H100s running at 80 percent utilization for a year, locking in a stable reserved rate instead of paying month-to-month on-demand pricing translates to over $73,000 in savings. That's a real number, not a marketing estimate, and it's the number that makes reserved pricing genuinely compelling for the right workload.

...

The discount percentage on a reserved contract directly sets the utilization rate you need to clear for reserving to pay off. The formula is straightforward: breakeven utilization equals one minus the discount percentage. A 40 percent reserved discount means you need roughly 60 percent utilization for reserving to beat on-demand. Most analysts converge on a similar range independently, generally recommending reserved capacity only once sustained utilization is expected to clear 55 to 70 percent for the full contract term.

Below that threshold, on-demand is very often the cheaper option even at its higher headline rate, because you're only paying for the hours you actually use. A reserved contract sitting idle a third of the time can end up costing more in total than simply paying the on-demand premium only when the GPU is genuinely working.

...

Reserved capacity is the clear winner for workloads with predictable, sustained demand: a production inference cluster serving real users around the clock runs at near-100 percent utilization by definition, and reserved pricing drops the effective cost by 35 to 55 percent with no change to how the system operates. Multi-week pre-training or fine-tuning runs with a known duration and continuous GPU usage fall into the same category, the runtime is predictable enough that locking in a rate is close to a free win.

On-demand wins when the opposite is true: early-stage testing, research sandboxes, and development environments typically run at 30 to 50 percent utilization, well under the breakeven threshold where reserving pays off. If your AI strategy is still evolving, or your project timeline is short enough that a 6 to 12 month commitment doesn't make sense, staying on-demand until you have real usage data to model against is the financially sound call, even with prices rising.

results.title: On Demand vs Spot Instances: GPU Cost Guide
highlights:
- On-demand instances give you stable capacity for workloads that should not be interrupted. Spot instances use discounted spare capacity, but the provider can reclaim that capacity.
- Spot is usually the lower hourly price, but the real cost depends on checkpointing, restart automation, persistent storage, queue delay, and missed deadlines.
- Use spot for checkpointed training, hyperparameter sweeps, stateless batch inference, and retryable batch jobs. Use on-demand for production inference, demos, active notebooks, and deadline-bound fine-tuning.
- A hybrid setup is often the most practical answer: keep a stable on-demand baseline, then add spot for elastic, retryable work.
- If interruption risk is the blocker, compare lower-cost on-demand GPU options before assuming spot is the only way to reduce spend.

...

On-demand instances are stable compute capacity you rent when you need predictable access; spot instances are discounted spare capacity that can be interrupted when the provider needs it back.

That difference drives the whole decision. On-demand is about control: you start the instance, keep it running, and pay the posted rate until you stop it. Spot is about price: you get a discount because the provider can reclaim the capacity.

...

Cloud providers use spot pricing to sell spare capacity that would otherwise sit idle. Because that capacity is not guaranteed, the provider can offer it below the regular on-demand price and reclaim it when demand changes.

The discount can be large. AWS says EC2 Spot Instances can be available at up to 90% off On-Demand pricing. Google Cloud says Spot VMs can offer up to 91% discounts for many machine types, GPUs, TPUs, and Local SSDs compared with on-demand standard VMs.

GPU-specific providers show the same tradeoff with their own rules. Hyperstack's GPU pricing page listed Spot VM H100 at $1.52 and A100 at $1.08. Novita's Spot GPU page listed RTX 4090 spot from $0.18/hour, up to 50% off, with 1-hour protection and 1-hour advance termination notice.

Those examples are useful, but they are not permanent claims. Spot prices, GPU availability, regions, and interruption terms can change. Treat every price as source- and date-bound, then re-check the current provider page before committing budget.

The durable idea is the pricing mechanism: spot is cheaper because it is less guaranteed. If your workload can treat reclaimed capacity as a normal event, the discount may be worth it. If it cannot, the lower hourly price is only part of the cost.

...

When interruption engineering is the problem, a lower-cost on-demand GPU can be the safer comparison point. For workloads that should not be built around reclaimed spare capacity, RunC.ai gives teams a stable GPU Pods option with dated public prices. RunC public pricing checked on 2026-06-26 lists:

results.title: GPU Leases Are Rising While Model Prices Fall
highlights:
For three years the advice was simple: if the API bill hurts, rent GPUs and serve the model yourself. That advice is quietly inverting. Per-token prices keep falling, while the compute you would rent to escape them is getting more expensive — Nvidia announced roughly a 20% rise on H100 rentals, and AWS put up H200 instance prices in January for the first time in about two decades. Here is the break-even arithmetic, and the honest caveat that these rises come off a crashed base.

...

## What changed

- Nvidia announced an approximately 20% price increase for H100 rentals in 2026. That is a stated move on rental pricing, not a market observation.
- Separately, market H100 rental costs have climbed by nearly 40% since October 2025. Different measurement, different mechanism — this is what the market has actually done, not what anyone announced.
- Separately again, H100 one-year lease contract prices rose approximately 40% over five months into early 2026. That is the contract market, and it is the one that carries lock-in risk.
- AWS raised H200 GPU instance prices by 15% on 4 January 2026. The `p5e.48xlarge`, which carries eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs, went from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour. It was the first GPU price increase in roughly two decades and broke a twenty-year precedent of cloud prices only ever going down.
- All of it comes off a collapsed base. H100 rental rates fell from roughly $8 per hour at their 2023 peak to as low as $1 to $2 per hour through the 2024-2025 oversupply. By early 2026 rates were still down roughly 64% to 75% from launch-era highs. A 40% rise from $2 an hour is not a return to $8.

...

## What you actually pay right now

The single most useful thing in this article is the spread. Before anyone debates leasing versus owning, look at how wide the same GPU-hour is priced across suppliers.

| Option | Headline rate | Per GPU-hour | Basis / source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 on-demand, full market range | $1.49 – $6.98 / hour | $1.49 – $6.98 | Varies by provider and commitment; bulk of the market clusters $2–$4 |
| H100 on-demand, budget tier | — | ~$2.85 – $3.50 | Budget-tier service average |
| H100 entry rate | — | from ~$2.01 | Provider-dependent starting price |
| A100 entry rate | — | from ~$1.09 | Provider-dependent starting price |
| GCP H100, `a3-highgpu-8g` | $80 – $90 / hour (8 GPUs) | ~$9.00 – $11.50 | On-demand list |
| AWS H200, `p5e.48xlarge` | $39.80 / hour (8 GPUs), up from $34.61 | ~$4.98 (was ~$4.33) | 15% increase effective 4 January 2026 |
| AWS per-GPU on-demand | — | ~$12.29 | Separate measurement to the p5e figure above — different instance basis |
| H100 one-year lease contract | No public rate card | Direction only | Contract prices up ~40% over five months into early 2026 |
| Owned hardware, effective all-in | — | ~$2.50 – $4.00 | Hardware amortised over 3 years, plus colocation and power, at 70% utilisation |

Read that table twice. The two AWS rows and the p5e row are measuring different things and must not be merged into one number — the $39.80 figure is an eight-H200 instance after a specific 15% rise, while the roughly $12.29 per-GPU figure is a separate on-demand measurement on a different basis. Similarly, the three headline percentage rises at the top of this piece are three distinct measurements of three distinct markets. Anyone adding them together to claim GPUs got 100% dearer is doing arithmetic on numbers that do not belong to each other.

What the table does show unambiguously is a four-to-eight times spread on the same class of silicon. A team paying hyperscaler list rates and complaining about GPU inflation has a much larger and much easier saving available than anything leasing or owning will produce.

...

The most expensive mistake available in 2026 is signing a multi-year lease at the top of a rising market on a utilisation figure you have assumed rather than measured. One-year H100 lease contract prices rose roughly 40% over five months into early 2026 — a contract signed against that level is priced off a spike, not a trend, and you carry it for the full term. Meanwhile the on-demand market still spans $1.49 to $6.98 per hour depending on provider and commitment, so the supplier spread is frequently wider than the discount a lease buys. Before committing, measure four weeks of real utilisation from production telemetry. If it is not comfortably above 70% and stable, do not lock the term.

results.title: KI-Hardware-Auktion: Fluence versteigert 6.000 GPUs ab August
highlights:
LONDON (IT BOLTWISE) – Die Mietpreise für KI-GPUs ziehen weiter an: Laut Branchenangaben haben sie sich binnen eines halben Jahres verdoppelt. Fluence startet ab dem 4. August GPU-Cluster-Auktionen, um Preistransparenz für reservierte Kapazitäten zu schaffen. Besonders betroffen sind Unternehmen, die H100- und Blackwell-Instanzen für Inferenz und Training nutzen. Gleichzeitig bleibt die Auslastung der Chips branchenweit laut den vorliegenden Zahlen niedrig, was das Preissignal zusätzlich verschärft.

KI-Hardware-Auktion: Fluence versteigert 6.000 GPUs ab August (Foto: IT BOLTWISE)

Der KI-Boom zeigt sich gerade weniger in neuen Modellen als in den Zeilen auf der Preistabelle: Innerhalb von nur einem halben Jahr sollen sich die Mietkosten für KI-Grafikprozessoren verdoppelt haben. Unternehmen zahlen den Angaben zufolge inzwischen rund vier US-Dollar pro Stunde für leistungsfähige GPU-Cluster. Für deutsche Anbieter und Anwendungsbetreiber ist das nicht nur eine operative Frage der Budgets, sondern auch eine Planungsfrage: Wenn Preis und Verfügbarkeit kurzfristig auseinanderlaufen, verschiebt sich der Aufwand von der Modellwahl hin zur Kapazitätsstrategie.

Im Zentrum steht dabei die Preisrallye entlang ganzer Chip-Generationen. NVIDIA H100-Modelle sollen im Januar noch unter zwei US-Dollar pro Stunde gekostet haben, im August seien es bereits rund drei US-Dollar gewesen. Bei den neuen Blackwell-Chips geht der Trend offenbar weiter: Für B200-Raten werden von „unter fünf“ US-Dollar im Vergleich zu bis zu 5,80 US-Dollar pro Stunde gesprochen. Diese Dynamik erfasst nicht nur ältere Bestände, sondern trifft auch auf die jüngsten, aktuell stark nachgefragten Plattformen.

Dass die Preisspirale kein reines Marktplatz-Phänomen ist, machen auch die großen Cloud-Anbieter sichtbar. So heißt es, Amazon Web Services habe die Preise für H200-Instanzen um 15 Prozent angehoben und mit einer p5e.48xlarge-Instanz einen konkreten Richtwert geliefert: 39,80 statt 34,61 US-Dollar pro Stunde. Auffällig ist jedoch die wirtschaftliche Spannung im System: Obwohl KI-Inferenz inzwischen 55 bis 80 Prozent der GPU-Ausgaben ausmache, liege die durchschnittliche Chip-Auslastung branchenweit nur bei etwa fünf Prozent. Genau diese Lücke zwischen Ausgaben und Nutzungsgrad verschärft die Kosten pro tatsächlich verarbeitetem Workload-Zyklus.

Neue Marktmechanismen entstehen genau deshalb: Fluence startet am 4. August GPU-Cluster-Auktionen, um Preistransparenz für reservierte Kapazitäten zu schaffen. Mehr als 6.000 GPUs in 13 Ländern sollen in diesen Auktionen verfügbar sein; genannt werden unter anderem Cluster in den USA, Kanada und Südkorea. Der Hintergrund ist laut den vorliegenden Informationen das Preisparadoxon zwischen Spot-Märkten und Vertragspreisen: Wenn Spot-Preise inzwischen häufig beim Doppelten der Vertragsraten liegen, wird planbare Nachfrage für Unternehmen wertvoller – und zugleich schwieriger, weil Reservierungen in der Knappheit ihren Preis finden. Für die KI-Betriebsplanung bedeutet das: Self-Serving reines „Kapazität sichern“ reicht oft nicht, wenn der Markt in Echtzeit umspringt.

results.title: The GPU You Can't Get: Why AI Deployment Timelines Slip on Capacity, Not Code
highlights:
That's not a hypothetical. According to Cast AI's 2026 platform telemetry across 23,000+ production clusters, average GPU utilization sits at 5%. On AKS it's 2%. On EKS, 5%. On GKE, 6%. A 20-GPU H100 cluster running at that utilization rate wastes roughly ~$168,000 per month (based on AWS p5.48xlarge on-demand pricing of ~$12.29/hr per H100). The GPUs are there. The money is leaving the account. The work isn't getting done.

...

AWS raised H200 Capacity Block prices 15% in January 2026. That's the first GPU price increase in over a decade of cloud GPU availability. When the cloud providers start raising prices on reserved compute, they're signaling that demand has outrun their ability to absorb it through efficiency gains alone.

...

AWS Capacity Blocks -- the mechanism for reserving GPU capacity in advance -- have become a reservation lottery. You submit a request for a future time window. If the block is available, you lock it in. If not, you wait and try again. For teams that need to scale training runs predictably, this is a real operational problem. Your deployment timeline depends on winning the lottery.

...

Fewer than 2% of GPU workloads run on Spot Instances, according to Cast AI's 2026 platform telemetry. That's a striking number given that H100 Spot prices in eu-north-1 dropped 88% between January 2024 and September 2025 -- from $105.20 to $12.16 per hour. The savings are available. The infrastructure to use them safely isn't in place for most teams.
